354.text: Assertion : Complexity of classification increases from kingdom to species.Reason : Common characters increase from kingdom to species.
options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion
If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion
If assertion is true but reason is false
If both assertion and reason are false
354.sol:
Classification involves hierarchy of steps, in which each step represents a rank or category, called taxonomic category or taxon. All taxa together constitute a taxonomic hierarchy as follows:
Species $\rightarrow$ Genus $\rightarrow$ Family $\rightarrow$ Order $\rightarrow$ Class $\rightarrow$ Phylum or division $\rightarrow$ Kingdom.
Most common characters among individual members are found in taxon species. Common characters decrease from species to kingdom and members of a kingdom have least number of common characters. Similarly, complexity of classification decreases from species to kingdom

1378.subject: Physics
1378.text: In an ideal parallel $L C$ circuit, the capacitor is charged by connecting it to a d.c. source which is then disconnected. The current in the circuit
1378.sol: When the capacitor is connected to a d.c. source and then disconnected, it gets charged and then it starts discharging through the inductor. An induced emf is produced in the circuit which opposes the growth of current in $L$. When the capacitor is fully discharged, the electric energy stored in the capacitor (i.e. $1 / 2 q^{2 / C}$ ) gets converted fully into magnetic field energy $\left(1 / 2 L I^2\right)$. As soon as the discharge of the capacitor is complete, current stops and the magnetic flux linked with $L$ starts collapsing. Therefore, an induced emf is again developed which starts recharging the capacitor in the opposite direction. When the recharging is completed, all magnetic energy stored in $L$ appears as the electric energy between the plates of the capacitor. The entire process keeps on repeating and the energy taken from the cell keeps on oscillating between $C and L$. Hence the current in the circuit starts oscillating as soon as the d.c. source charging the capacitor is disconnected.

1797.text: A disc of radius $20 \mathrm{~cm}$ and mass $1 / 2 \mathrm{~kg}$ is rolling on an inclined plane. Find out the frictional force such that disc performs pure rolling.
1797.sol: Let $m$ be the mass and $R$ be the radius of the disc. $m g \sin \theta-f=m a_{c m} \begin{aligned} & \tau_{c m}=I_{c m^\alpha} \\ & f R=\frac{m R^2}{2}\left(\frac{a_{c m}}{R}\right)\end{aligned} f=\frac{m a_{c m}}{2} or a_{c m}=\frac{2 f}{m}$ So, $m g \sin \theta-f=m\left(\frac{2 f}{m}\right) f=\frac{m g \sin \theta}{3}=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{10}{3} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{5}{3 \sqrt{2}} \mathrm{~N}$

1935.text: Which one is correct regarding electrocardiograph (ECG)?
options: P-wave represents the electrical excitation of the ventricle.
QRS complex represents repolarisation of the ventricles.
T-wave represents repolarisation of the atria.
By counting the number of QRS complexes one can determine the pulse rate.
1935.sol: The P-wave represents the electrical excitation (or depolarisation) of the atria, which leads to the contraction of both the atria. The QRS complex represents the depolarisation of the ventricles, which initiates the ventricular contraction. The Twave represents the return of the ventricles from excited to normal state (repolarisation). So, by counting the number of QRS complexes that occur in a given time period, one can determine the heart beat rate of an individual.

2017.subject: Zoology
2017.text: A person passes much urine and drinks much water but his blood glucose level is normal. This condition may be the result of :
options: a reduction in insulin secretion from pancreas
a reduction in vasopressin secretion from posterior pituitary
a fall in the glucose concentration in urine
an increase in secretion of glucagon.
2017.sol: Vasopressin or $\mathrm{ADH}$ secreted from posterior pituitary stimulates reabsorption of water by the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting renal tubules and thus regulates urine volume. It has no such important effect on glucose metabolism. Therefore, a person whose blood glucose level is normal, but passes much urine and drinks much water has a reduction in vasopressin secretion which ultimately leads to diabetes insipidus.

9050.text: $If the eccentricity of a hyperbola is \dfrac{5}{3},$ then the eccentricity of its conjugate hyperbola is
9050.sol:
Let the eccentricity of hyperbola and conjugate hyperbola be ${e}_{1} \text{ and } {e}_{2}$ respectively. Then,

$1{e}_{1}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{e}_{2}^{2}} = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)^{2}} + 1{e}_{2}^{2} = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{9}{25} + 1{e}_{2}^{2} = 1$

$⇒ 1{e}_{2}^{2} = 1 - \dfrac{9}{25}$

$⇒ 1{e}_{2}^{2} = \dfrac{16}{25}$

$⇒ {e}_{2} = \pm \dfrac{5}{4}$

But, eccentricity of hyperbola is never less than one. Hence, ${e}_{2} = \dfrac{5}{4}$.

13713.subject: Physics
13713.text:
Assertion (A) Two condensers of same capacity are connected first in parallel and then in series. The ratio of resultant capacities in the two cases will be $4: 1$.
Reason (R$ ) In parallel, capacity increases and in series capacity decreases.$
options: Both $A$ and $R$ are true and $R$ is a correct explanation for $\mathrm{A}$.
Both $A$ and $R$ are true but $R$ is not a correct explanation for A.
13713.sol:
Given, two capacitors of same capacities $C$.
In series, equivalent capacitance is given by
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{C_S}=\frac{1}{C_1}+\frac{1}{C_2}=\frac{1}{C}+\frac{1}{C}=\frac{2}{C} \\ & C_S=\frac{C}{2}\end{aligned}$
In parallel, equivalent capacitance is given by
$C_P=C_1+C_2=C+C=2 C$
Ratio $=\frac{C_P}{C_S}=\frac{2 C}{\left(\frac{C}{2}\right)}=\frac{4}{1}\Rightarrow \quad C_P: C_S=4: 1$
Hence, Assertion is true
In parallel, $C_P > C$
In series, $C_S < C$
So, in parallel, capacity is increased but in series, capacity is decreased.
Hence, Reason is also true, but it is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

or $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{a}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{gsin\theta}}$ [for smooth plane]

For the rough plane. the effective value of acceleration along the incline is
$a^{'} = gsin\theta - {μ}_{k}gcos\theta$

and $t^{'} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{a}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2s}{gsin\theta - {μ}_{k}gcos\theta}}$

Now, $\dfrac{t '}{t} = n = \sqrt{\dfrac{gsin\theta}{gsin\theta - {μ}_{k}gcos\theta}}$

$= \sqrt{\dfrac{sin45 °}{sin45 ° - {μ}_{k}cos45 °}}$

$= \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{1 - {μ}_{k}}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{n2} = 1 - {μ}_{k} ⇒ {μ}_{k} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{n2}$

20649.subject: Chemistry
20649.text:
A solution of $\mathrm{KCl}(\mathrm{M}=74.5 \mathrm{ g} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1})$ containing $1.9 \mathrm{ g}$ per $100 \mathrm{ mL}$ of $\mathrm{KCl}$ is isotonic with a solution of urea $(\mathrm{M}=60.0 \mathrm{ g} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1}$) containing $3 \mathrm{ g}$ per $100 \mathrm{ mL}$ of urea. The degree of dissociation of $\mathrm{KCl}$ is:
[Assume both the solutions are kept at same temperature]
20649.sol:
For two isotonic solutions at the same temperature, the osmotic pressures are equal, which implies their molar concentrations are equal when accounting for the van't Hoff factor $i$.

The molar concentration of the KCl solution is $C_1 = \dfrac{1.9 \text{ g} / 74.5 \text{ g mol}^{-1}}{0.1 \text{ L}} = \dfrac{1.9}{7.45} \text{ M} \approx 0.255 \text{ M}$.

The molar concentration of the urea solution is $C_2 = \dfrac{3 \text{ g} / 60.0 \text{ g mol}^{-1}}{0.1 \text{ L}} = \dfrac{3}{6} \text{ M} = 0.5 \text{ M}$.

Since urea is a non-electrolyte, its van't Hoff factor $i_2 = 1$. For KCl, which dissociates as $\text{KCl} \rightarrow \textK^{+} + \text{Cl}^{-}$, the van't Hoff factor is $i_1 = 1 + \alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the degree of dissociation.

The condition for isotonic solutions is $i_1 C_1 = i_2 C_2$.

Substituting the values: $(1 + \alpha) \times \left( \dfrac{1.9}{7.45} \right) = 1 \times 0.5$.

$1 + \alpha = 0.5 \times \left( \dfrac{7.45}{1.9} \right) = \dfrac{3.725}{1.9} \approx 1.9605$.

$\alpha = 1.9605 - 1 = 0.9605$.

Rounding to the nearest given option, $\alpha = 0.96$.

Answer: 0.96

21525.text:
The sum of three numbers is 20.
If we multiply the first number by 2 and add the second number to the result, and subtract the third number, we get 23.
By adding second and third numbers to three times the first number, we get 46.
The above situation can be represented in matrix form as $A X=B$ then the value of determinant formed by the cofactors of matrix A is
21525.sol:
Let the three numbers be $x, y, z$. The given conditions are:

$x + y + z = 20$
$2x + y - z = 23$
$3x + y + z = 46$

The matrix $A$ is given by:
$A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$

The determinant of $A$ is $|A| = 1(1 - (-1)) - 1(2 - (-3)) + 1(2 - 3) = 1(2) - 1(5) + 1(-1) = 2 - 5 - 1 = -4$.

Let $C$ be the matrix of cofactors of $A$. The determinant of the cofactor matrix is given by $|C| = |A|^{n-1}$, where $n$ is the order of the matrix. Here $n = 3$.

$|C| = |A|^{3-1} = |A|^2$.

Substituting $|A| = -4$, we get $|C| = (-4)^2 = 16$.

Answer: 16

21826.text: The range of the function $f(x) = {}^{(7-x)}P_{(x-3)}$ is
21826.sol:
For $f(x) = {}^{(7-x)}P_{(x-3)}$ to be defined, the following conditions must be satisfied:

$7 - x \ge 0 \Rightarrow x \le 7$

$x - 3 \ge 0 \Rightarrow x \ge 3$

$7 - x \ge x - 3 \Rightarrow 2x \le 10 \Rightarrow x \le 5$

Also, $x$ must be an integer.

From the above inequalities, the possible values of $x$ are $3, 4, 5$.

Substituting these values into the function:

For $x = 3$, $f(3) = {}^{4}P_{0} = 1$

For $x = 4$, $f(4) = {}^{3}P_{1} = 3$

For $x = 5$, $f(5) = {}^{2}P_{2} = 2$

Therefore, the range of the function is $\{1, 2, 3\}$.

Answer: $\{1, 2, 3\}$

21849.text: A candidate is required to answer 7 questions out of 12 questions which are divided into two groups each containing 6 questions. He is not permitted to attempt more than 5 questions from either group. The number of ways in which he can choose the 7 question is
21849.sol:
The total number of questions is 12, divided into two groups of 6 questions each. Let the groups be A and B, each containing 6 questions. The candidate needs to select 7 questions in total, with the constraint that no more than 5 questions can be selected from either group.

Let $x$ be the number of questions selected from group A and $y$ be the number of questions selected from group B. We have $x + y = 7$ and the constraints $x \le 5$ and $y \le 5$.

Possible pairs $(x, y)$ satisfying these conditions are:
1. $x = 2, y = 5$: The number of ways is ^{6}C_{2} \times ^{6}C_{5} = 15 \times 6 = 90$.
2. $x = 3, y = 4$: The number of ways is ^{6}C_{3} \times ^{6}C_{4} = 20 \times 15 = 300$.
3. $x = 4, y = 3$: The number of ways is ^{6}C_{4} \times ^{6}C_{3} = 15 \times 20 = 300$.
4. $x = 5, y = 2$: The number of ways is ^{6}C_{5} \times ^{6}C_{2} = 6 \times 15 = 90$.

Summing these possibilities, the total number of ways is $90 + 300 + 300 + 90 = 780$.

Answer: 780

22481.text:
A network of capacitors is as shown below. If the voltage supply is 100 V , find the energy stored in the $6 \mu \mathrm{ F}$ capacitor.
$C_1=3 \mu F, C_2=6 \mu F, C_3=3 \mu F$ and $C_4=4 \mu F$
22481.sol:
The circuit consists of a capacitor $C_4$ in parallel with the series combination of $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3$.

First, calculate the equivalent capacitance of the series branch containing $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3$. Let this be $C_{series}$.

$\dfrac{1}{C_{series}} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} + \dfrac{1}{C_3} = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2+1+2}{6} = \dfrac{5}{6} \mu F^{-1}$

$C_{series} = \dfrac{6}{5} = 1.2 \mu F$

The voltage across the series branch is equal to the supply voltage $V = 100 V$.

The charge $Q$ on the series branch is $Q = C_{series} \times V = 1.2 \mu F \times 100 V = 120 \mu C$.

Since $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3$ are in series, they all carry the same charge $Q = 120 \mu C$.

The energy stored in the $C_2 = 6 \mu F$ capacitor is given by $U = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C_2}$.

$U = \dfrac{(120 \times 10^{-6})^2}{2 \times 6 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{14400 \times 10^{-12}}{12 \times 10^{-6}} = 1200 \times 10^{-6} J = 1.2 \times 10^{-3} J = 1.2 mJ$.

Answer: 1.2 mJ

22830.text: A tiny ball of mass $\mathrm{m}$ and charge $\mathrm{q}$ is suspended from the fixed support using an insulating string of length $1 \mathrm{ m}$. The horizontal uniform electric field $\mathrm{E}$ is switched on. The angle made by the string with vertical when the ball is in equilibrium is $45^{{}^{\circ}}$. The magnitude of uniform electric field is
22830.sol:
Let the mass of the ball be $m$, charge be $q$, and the electric field be $E$. The forces acting on the ball in equilibrium are:

1. Gravitational force $mg$ acting vertically downwards.
2. Electric force $qE$ acting horizontally.
3. Tension $T$ in the string acting along the string at an angle $\theta = 45^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the vertical.

Resolving the forces into horizontal and vertical components:

Horizontal direction: $T \sin \theta = qE$

Vertical direction: $T \cos \theta = mg$

Dividing the two equations:

$\dfrac{T \sin \theta}{T \cos \theta} = \dfrac{qE}{mg}$

$\tan \theta = \dfrac{qE}{mg}$

Given $\theta = 45^{{}^{\circ}}$, we have $\tan 45^{{}^{\circ}} = 1$.

$1 = \dfrac{qE}{mg}$

$E = \dfrac{mg}{q}$

Answer: $E=\dfrac{m g}{q} \quad N C^{-1}$

23003.subject: Physics
23003.text: The magnetic field at the centre of a wire loop formed by two semicircular wires of radii $r_1$ = 3.14m and $r_2$ = 6.28m and carrying a current of I =2A is:
23003.sol:
The magnetic field at the centre of the loop is the vector sum of the magnetic fields produced by the four segments of the wire: two straight segments and two semicircular arcs.

For the straight segments, the line of action of the current passes through the centre of the loop. Therefore, the angle between the current element $d\vec{l}$ and the position vector $\vec{r}$ is $0$ or $\pi$. The magnetic field due to these segments at the centre is zero.

For the semicircular arcs, the magnetic field at the centre is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4r}$.

The current in the larger semicircle of radius $r_2$ flows in the counter-clockwise direction. By the right-hand thumb rule, its magnetic field at the centre is directed outwards (out of the page).
$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4r_2}$

The current in the smaller semicircle of radius $r_1$ also flows in the counter-clockwise direction. Its magnetic field at the centre is also directed outwards.
$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4r_1}$

Since both magnetic fields are in the same direction, the net magnetic field at the centre is their sum:
$B_{\text{net}} = B_1 + B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4} \left( \dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2} \right)

Given:
$ I = 2$\text{ A}
$ r_1 = 3.14$\text{ m} \approx \pi\text{ m}
$ r_2 = 6.28$\text{ m} \approx2\pi\text{ m}
$\mu_0 = 4$\pi \times10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}

Substituting the values:
$ B_{$\text{net}$} = $\dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2}{4} \left( \dfrac{1}{\pi} + \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \right)

B_{\text{net}$} = $2\pi \times10^{-7} \left( \dfrac{2 + 1}{2\pi} \right)$

$B_{\text{net}} = 2\pi \times10^{-7} \left( \dfrac{3}{2\pi} \right)

B_{\text{net}$} = 3 $\times10^{-7}\text{ T}

Answer: 3 \times10^{-7}\ T$

23113.text: Forces A and B act at a point. The sum of their magnitudes is 50 N and the magnitude of their resultant is 20 N. If the resultant is at $90^{}^{\circ}$ with the smaller force, the magnitudes of A and B, in N are
23113.sol:
Let the magnitudes of the two forces be $F_1$ and $F_2$ with $F_1 < F_2$.

Given that the sum of their magnitudes is $50\ \text{N}$:
$F_1 + F_2 = 50$

The resultant $R$ is perpendicular to the smaller force $F_1$. The angle $\alpha$ made by the resultant with $F_1$ is given by:
$\tan \alpha = \dfrac{F_2 \sin \theta}{F_1 + F_2 \cos \theta}$

Since $\alpha = 90^{}^{\circ}$, the denominator must be zero:
$F_1 + F_2 \cos \theta = 0 \Rightarrow \cos \theta = -\dfrac{F_1}{F_2}$

The magnitude of the resultant is given by:
$R^2 = F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2F_1 F_2 \cos \theta$

Substituting $\cos \theta = -\dfrac{F_1}{F_2}$ and $R = 20\ \text{N}$:
$20^2 = F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2F_1 F_2 \left(-\dfrac{F_1}{F_2}\right)
400 = F_1^2 + F_2^2 - 2F_1^2$
$F_2^2 - F_1^2 = 400$
$(F_2 - F_1)(F_2 + F_1) = 400$

Substituting $F_1 + F_2 = 50$ into the equation:
$(F_2 - F_1)(50) = 400$
$F_2 - F_1 = 8$

Solving the two equations $F_2 + F_1 = 50$ and $F_2 - F_1 = 8$ simultaneously:
$2F_2 = 58 \Rightarrow F_2 = 29\ \text{N}
2F_1 = 42 \Rightarrow F_1 = 21\ \text{N}

The magnitudes of the forces are 29\ \text{N} and 21\ \text{N}.

Answer: 29\text{N},\ 21\text{N}$

23848.subject: Biology
23848.text: Which one of the following correctly describes the mode of action of Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH) and estrogen?
options: FSH interacts with membrane-bound receptor and generates cyclic AMP, while estrogen interacts with intracellular receptor and regulates gene expression
Both FSH and estrogen regulate gene expression via intracellular receptors
FSH interacts with intracellular receptor and generates cyclic AMP, while estrogen interacts with membrane-bound receptor and regulates cellular metabolism
Both FSH and estrogen regulate cellular metabolism via membrane-bound receptors
23848.sol:
FSH is a proteinaceous hormone that cannot pass through the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane. It binds to specific membrane-bound receptors on the target cell surface, leading to the generation of second messengers like cyclic AMP (cAMP), which in turn regulate cellular metabolism.

Estrogen is a steroid hormone and is lipid-soluble. It easily diffuses across the cell membrane and binds to intracellular receptors (usually in the nucleus). The hormone-receptor complex then interacts with the genome to regulate gene expression or chromosome function.

Answer: FSH interacts with membrane-bound receptor and generates cyclic AMP, while estrogen interacts with intracellular receptor and regulates gene expression

25345.text: Let $\omega \ne 1$ be a cube root of unity. Then the minimum of the set ${ {\left|a + b\omega + c{\omega}^{2}\right|}^{2}: a, b, c$ distinct non$–$zero integers $}$ equals ________

If $z$ is a complex number
Then $| z{|}^{2} = z\overset{¯}{z}$
Now,
${\left|a + b\omega + c{\omega}^{2}\right|$}^{2} = $\left(a + b\omega + c{\omega}^{2}\right)\left(\overset{¯}{a + b\omega + c{\omega}^{2}}\right)
${$\left|a + b\omega + c{\omega}^{2}\right|$}^{2} = $\left(a + b\omega + c{\omega}^{2}\right)\left(a + b\overset{-}{\omega} + c{\overset{-}{\omega}}^{2}\right)
\left(ifa \in R ⇒ \overset{-}{a} = a\right)
\left(\overset{¯}{{z}_{1}{z}_{2}} = \overset{-}{z}1\overset{-}{z}2\right)
\left(\overset{-}{\omega} = {\omega}^{2}, {\overset{-}{\omega}}^{2} = \omega\right)


${$\left|a + b\omega + c{\omega}^{2}\right|$}^{2} = $\left(a + b\omega + c{\omega}^{2}\right)\left(a + b{\omega}^{2} + c\omega\right)
$= $\left({a}^{2} + {b}^{2} + {c}^{2} - ab - bc - ca\right)$
$\left(\text{∵}{\omega}^{3} = 1, 1 + \omega + {\omega}^{2} = 0\right)$
$| a + b\omega + c{\omega}^{2}{|}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} [ {\left(a - b\right)}^{2} + {\left(b - c\right)}^{2} + {\left(c - a\right)}^{2} ]$

26122.subject: Physics
26122.text:
A Hydrogen-like atom has atomic number $Z$. Photons emitted in the electronic transitions from level $n = 4$ to level $n = 3$ in these atoms are used to perform photoelectric effect experiment on a target metal. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons generated is $1 . 95eV$. If the photoelectric threshold wavelength for the target metal is $310nm$, the value of $Z$ is _____.

[Given $hc = 1240eV - nm$ and $Rhc = 13 . 6eV$, where $R$ is the Rydberg constant, $h$ is the Planck’s constant and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum]
26122.sol:
From Einstein's photoelectric effect, we can write

$E = K{E}_{max} + ϕ ⇒ E = K{E}_{max} + \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$

$⇒ ∆ {E}_{4to3} = 1 . 95eV + \dfrac{1240}{310}eV ⇒ ∆ {E}_{4to3} = 5 . 95eV$

Now, as we know for Hydrogen like atoms, we can write $∆ E = 13 . 6{Z}^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{{\left({n}_{1}\right)}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{\left({n}_{2}\right)}^{2}}\right)$

Therefore,$⇒ 13 . 6{Z}^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{{3}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{4}^{2}}\right) = 5 . 95$

$⇒ 13 . 6{Z}^{2}\dfrac{7}{9 \times 16} = 5 . 95$

$⇒ {Z}^{2} = \dfrac{5 . 95 \times 9 \times 16}{13 . 6 \times 7} = 9$

$⇒ Z = 3$

26322.subject: Physics
26322.text: An $\alpha$-particle (mass $4$ amu) and a singly charged Sulphur ion (mass $32$ amu) are initially at rest. They are accelerated through a potential $V$ and then allowed to pass into a region of uniform magnetic field which is normal to the velocities of the particles. Within this region, the $\alpha$-particle and the sulphur ion move in circular orbits of radii ${R}_{\alpha} and {R}_{S}$, respectively. The ratio $\left(\dfrac{{R}_{S}}{{R}_{\alpha}}\right)$ is __________ .
26322.sol:
When a particle moves on a circular path in a magnetic field then,

$∵ R = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mE}}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mqV}}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mV}}{\sqrt{q}B}$

According to given data,

$∵ V = \text{constant}\text{\text{ and }}B = \text{constant}$

$∴ R ∝ \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{q}}$

$\dfrac{{R}_{\alpha}}{{R}_{S}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{m}_{\alpha}}{{q}_{\alpha}} \times \dfrac{{q}_{S}}{{m}_{S}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{32}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{R}_{\alpha}}{{R}_{S}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{16}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Then, $\dfrac{{R}_{S}}{{R}_{\alpha}} = 4$

26563.text: Two transparent media of refractive indices $\mu_1$ and $\mu_3$ have a solid lens shaped transparent material of refractive index $\mu_2$ between them as shown in figures in Column II. A ray traversing these media is also shown in the figures. In Column I different relationships between $\mu_1, \mu_2$ and $\mu_3$ are given. Match them to the ray diagram shown in Column II.
options:
(A) P,R, (B) Q,S,T, (C) P,R,T, (D) Q,S

(A) P, (B) Q,S, (C) P,R,T, (D) Q,R,S

(A) P,R, (B) Q,S, (C) P,T, (D) Q,R,S

(A) P, (B) Q,S,T, (C) P,T, (D) Q,S
26563.sol:
(A) $\rightarrow$ since $\mu_1 < \mu_2$, the ray of light will bend towards normal after first refraction.
(B) $\rightarrow \mu_1>\mu_2$, the ray of light will bend away from the normal after first refraction.
(C) $\rightarrow$ since $\mu_2=\mu_3$ means in second refraction there will be no change in the path of ray of light.
(D) $\rightarrow$ Since $\mu_2>\mu_3$, ray of light will bend away from the normal after second refraction.
Therefore the correct options are as under.
(A) $\rightarrow$ P, R
(B) $\rightarrow$ Q, S, T
(C) $\rightarrow$ P, R, T
(D) $\rightarrow$ Q, $S$

27831.subject: Chemistry
27831.text:
Amongst the following the number of oxide(s) which are paramagnetic in nature is

${Na}_{2}O, {KO}_{2}, {NO}_{2}, {N}_{2}O, {ClO}_{2}, NO, {SO}_{2}, {Cl}_{2}O$
27831.sol:
The magnetic properties of a substance can be determined by examining its electron configuration: If it has unpaired electrons, then the substance is paramagnetic and if all electrons are paired, the substance is then diamagnetic.

${KO}_{2}$ is potassium superoxide. There is one unpaired electron in anti-bonding molecular orbital of superoxide. Potassium superoxide is paramagnetic due to the presence of unpaired electron.

${NO}_{2}, {ClO}_{2}, NO$ are odd electron species. Hence, they are paramagnetic.

The other are monoxide and dioxide contain paired electrons, so they will show diamagnetic behaviour.

29636.subject: Chemistry
29636.text: Identify the correct IUPAC name of hydrocarbon ($x$) containing three primary carbon atoms and with molar mass $72\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
29636.sol:
Let the hydrocarbon be an alkane with general formula $C_nH_{2n+2}$.

Molar mass $= 14n + 2 = 72 \Rightarrow 14n = 70 \Rightarrow n = 5$

The molecular formula is $C_5H_{12}$.

The structural isomers of $C_5H_{12}$ are:

n-pentane: $CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3$ (2 primary carbons)

2-methylbutane: $CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_3$ (3 primary carbons)

2,2-dimethylpropane: $C(CH_3)_4$ (4 primary carbons)

The hydrocarbon with exactly three primary carbon atoms is 2-methylbutane.

Answer: 2-Methylbutane

30471.text: $3 -$Methylhex-2-ene on reaction with $HBr$ in presence of peroxide forms an addition product (A). The number of possible stereoisomers for ' $A$ ' is ________.
30471.sol:
The hydrogen bromide addition in peroxides follows Anti Markovnikov rule.  Anti Markovnikov  addition reaction is found to follow a free radical mechanism. The peroxide compound involved helps in the generation of free radicals. The Anti-Markovnikov rule defines regiochemistry in which the substituent is attached to a less substituted carbon instead of the more substituted carbon.

The reaction of $3 -$Methylhex-2-ene  with $HBr$ in presence of peroxide, takes place as follows,

$2$ chiral carbons, here, so, total number of stereoisomers will be ${2}^{n} = {2}^{2} = 4$

30903.text: Consider the oxides of group $14$ elements $Si{O}_{2}, Ge{O}_{2}, Sn{O}_{2}, Pb{O}_{2}, CO$ and $GeO$. The amphoteric oxides are
30903.sol:
All members of group 14 when heated in oxygen form oxides. There are mainly two types of oxides, i.e., monoxide and dioxide of formula $MO$ and ${MO}_{2}$ respectively. $SiO$ only exists at high temperature. Oxides in higher oxidation states of elements are generally more acidic than those in lower oxidation states. The dioxides ${CO}_{2}, {SiO}_{2}$ and ${GeO}_{2}$ are acidic, whereas ${SnO}_{2}$ and ${PbO}_{2}$ are amphoteric in nature. Amongst monoxides, $CO$ is neutral.

Hence option C is the answer.

Curve $x = 12\left(t + sintcost\right)$

Now $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{\dfrac{dy}{dt}}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}}$

$tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(12{\left(1 + sint\right)}^{2}\right)}{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(12\left(t + sintcost\right)\right)}$

$\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{12 \times 2\left(1 + sint\right)\left(cost\right)}{12\left(1 + cos2t\right)}$

$\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{2\left(1 + sint\right) \cdot cost}{2\cos^{2}t}$

$\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{1 + sint}{cost} = \dfrac{{\left(cos\dfrac{t}{2} + sin\dfrac{t}{2}\right)}^{2}}{\cos^{2}\dfrac{t}{2} - \sin^{2}\dfrac{t}{2}}$

$\sqrt{3} = tan\left(\dfrac{t}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$

$\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{t}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{4} ⇒ \dfrac{t}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{12} ⇒ t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

Now putting $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ in $y = 12{\left(1 + sint\right)}^{2}$

as $\left({x}_{0}, {y}_{0}\right)$ lie on curve

So ${y}_{0} = 12{\left(1 + sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)}^{2}$

$= 12{\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)}^{2} = 27$

33831.text: Let $z = a + ib, b \ne 0$ be complex numbers satisfying ${z}^{2} = \overset{¯}{z} \cdot {2}^{1 - \left|z\right|}$. Then the least value of $n \in N$, such that ${z}^{n} = {\left(z + 1\right)}^{n}$, is equal to _____ .
33831.sol:
Given,

${z}^{2} = \overset{¯}{z} \cdot {2}^{1 - \left|z\right|} ⋯ \left(1\right)$

On taking modulus both side we get,

$⇒ {\left|z\right|}^{2} = \left|z\right| \cdot {2}^{1 - \left|z\right|}$

$⇒ \left|z\right| = {2}^{1 - \left|z\right|}, ∵ b \ne 0 ⇒ \left|z\right| \ne 0$

So comparing both side we get $\left|z\right| = 1 ⋯ \left(2\right)$

Now putting $z = a + ib$ then $\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}} = 1 ⋯ \left(3\right)$

Now again from equation $\left(1\right)$, equation $\left(2\right)$, equation $\left(3\right)$ we get:

${a}^{2} - {b}^{2} + i2ab = \left(a - ib\right){2}^{0} = a - ib$

Now on comaparing imagenary and real part we get,

$∴ {a}^{2} - {b}^{2} = a$ and $2ab = - b$

Now solving we get, $a = - \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $b = \pm \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

So, $z = - \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i$ or $= - \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i$

Now solving ${z}^{n} = {\left(z + 1\right)}^{n} ⇒ {\left(\dfrac{z + 1}{z}\right)}^{n} = 1$

$⇒ {\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{z}\right)}^{n} = 1$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{3}i}{2}\right)}^{n} = 1$

$⇒ {\left(- {\omega}^{2}\right)}^{n} = 1$, then minimum value of $n$ is $6$

34073.text: Let $f: R \to R$ be differentiable at $c \in R$ and $f\left(c\right) = 0$. If $g\left(x\right) = \left|f\left(x\right)\right|$, then at $x = c, g$ is:
34073.sol:
Given $g\left(x\right) = \left|f\left(x\right)\right|$ and $f\left(c\right) = 0$

${g}^{'}\left({c}^{+}\right) = \lim_{x \to {c}^{+}}\dfrac{\left|f\left(x\right)\right| - f\left(c\right)}{x - c} = \lim_{x \to {c}^{+}}\left|\dfrac{f\left(x\right) - f ( c )}{x - c}\right|, asx > c$

$⇒ {g}^{'}\left({c}^{+}\right) = \left|{f}^{'}\left(c\right)\right|$

$g\left({c}^{-}\right) = \lim_{x \to {c}^{-}}\dfrac{\left|f\left(x\right)\right| - f\left(c\right)}{x - c} = - \lim_{x \to {c}^{-}}\left|\dfrac{f\left(x\right) - f ( c )}{x - c}\right|, asx < c$

$⇒ {g}^{'}\left({c}^{-}\right) = - \left|{f}^{'}\left(c\right)\right|$

For $g\left(x\right)$ to be differentiable at $x = c$, ${f}^{'}\left(c\right)$ must be $0$. Else, it is non-differentiable.

\left(gof\right)\left(b\right) = gof\left(3\right) = g\left(3\right) = 32$

35746.text: If the value of $\lim_{x \to 0}{\left(2 - cosx\sqrt{cos2x}\right)}^{\left(\dfrac{x + 2}{{x}^{2}}\right)}$ is equal to ${e}^{a}$, then $a$ is equal to_____.
35746.sol:
We have,

$\lim_{x \to 0}{\left(2 - cosx\sqrt{cos2x}\right)}^{\left(\dfrac{x + 2}{{x}^{2}}\right)} \to {1}^{\infty}$

Hence,
$= {e}^{\lim_{x \to 0}\left(\dfrac{1 - cosx\sqrt{cos2x}}{{x}^{2}}\right) \times \left(x + 2\right)}$
Now,

$\lim_{x \to 0}\left(\dfrac{1 - cosx\sqrt{cos2x}}{{x}^{2}}\right) \to \left(\dfrac{0}{0}\right)$

Using L'Hospital Rule

$\lim_{x \to 0}\left\{\dfrac{sinx\sqrt{cos2x} - cosx \times \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{cos2x}} \times \left(- 2sin2x\right)}{2x}\right\}$

$= \lim_{x \to 0}\left\{\dfrac{sinxcos2x + sin2x \cdot cosx}{2x\sqrt{cos2x}}\right\}$

$= \lim_{x \to 0}\left\{\dfrac{sin3x}{2x\sqrt{cos2x}}\right\}$

$= \dfrac{3}{2}\lim_{x \to 0}\left\{\dfrac{sin3x}{3x}\right\} \times \lim_{x \to 0}\left\{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{cos2x}}\right\}$

$= \dfrac{3}{2}\lim_{x \to 0}\left\{\dfrac{sin3x}{3x}\right\} \times 1$

$= \dfrac{3}{2}$

So,

${e}^{\lim_{x \to 0}\left(\dfrac{1 - cosx\sqrt{cos2x}}{{x}^{2}}\right)\left(x + 2\right)}$

$= {e}^{\dfrac{3}{2} \times 2} = {e}^{3}$

$⇒ a = 3$

So, $A + B = \left(\begin{cases}2 & - 2 \\ 1 & - 1\end{cases}\right) + \left(\begin{cases}- 1 & 2 \\ - 1 & 2\end{cases}\right) = \left(\begin{cases}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{cases}\right) = I$

$⇒ \dfrac{\lambda}{1 - \dfrac{1}{2}} = 1 ⇒ \lambda = \dfrac{1}{2}$

So, $P\left({w}_{n}\right) = \dfrac{1}{{2}^{n}}$

$A = \left\{2k + 3l; k, l \in N\right\} = \left\{5, 7, 8, 9, 10 \ldots \ldots\right\}$

$B = \left\{{w}_{5}, {w}_{7}, {w}_{8}, {w}_{9}, {w}_{10}, {w}_{11}, \ldots\right\}$

$A = \mathbb{N} - \left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6\right\}$

$∴ P\left(B\right) = 1 - \left[P\left({w}_{1}\right) + P\left({w}_{2}\right) + P\left({w}_{3}\right) + P\left({w}_{4}\right) + P\left({w}_{6}\right)\right]$

$= 1 - \left[\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{16} + \dfrac{1}{64}\right]$

$= 1 - \left(\dfrac{32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1}{64}\right) = \dfrac{3}{64}$

If M is the mutual inductance, then

$M\dfrac{d i}{d t} = \dfrac{d ϕ}{d t} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}{\mu}_{0}{R}^{2}}{L}\dfrac{di}{dt}$

$⇒ M = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}{\mu}_{0}{R}^{2}}{L}$

40456.text:
Consider two identical metallic spheres of radius $R$ each having charge $Q$ and mass $m$. Their centers have an initial separation of $4 R$. Both the spheres are given an initial speed of $u$ towards each other. The minimum value of $u$, so that they can just touch each other is :
(Take $k=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}}$ and assume $k Q^{2}>G m^{2}$ where $G$ is the Gravitational constant)
options: $\sqrt{\frac{k Q^{2}}{2 m R}\left(1-\frac{G m^{2}}{2 k Q^{2}}\right)}$
40456.sol:
Using energy conservation, the system's kinetic energy must overcome the increase in electrostatic potential energy as the spheres approach.
Initial state: separation 4R, speed u each.
Final state: touching (separation 2R), speed zero.
Change in potential energy: $\Delta U = k\frac{Q^2}{2R} - k\frac{Q^2}{4R} = k\frac{Q^2}{4R}$.
Initial kinetic energy: $KE_i = mu^2$.
Energy equation: $mu^2 = k\frac{Q^2}{4R}\left(1 - \frac{Gm^2}{kQ^2}\right)$.
Therefore, $u = \sqrt{\frac{kQ^2}{4mR}\left(1 - \frac{Gm^2}{kQ^2}\right)}$.

$= \sqrt{1 . 6 \times 4 \times {10}^{13}} = 4 \times 2 \times {10}^{6}m{s}^{- 1}$

40738.text: In a screw gauge when the circular scale is given five complete rotations it moves linearly by $2.5$ mm. If the circular scale has $100$ divisions, the least count of screw gauge is _____ mm.
40738.sol:
Pitch of the screw gauge is the linear distance moved in one complete rotation.

$\text{Pitch} = \dfrac{2.5}{5} = 0.5 \text{ mm}$

Least count of the screw gauge is given by the ratio of the pitch to the total number of divisions on the circular scale.

$\text{Least count} = \dfrac{\text{Pitch}}{\text{Number of divisions on circular scale}}$

$\text{Least count} = \dfrac{0.5}{100} = 0.005 \text{ mm}$

$\text{Least count} = 5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mm}$

Answer: $5 \times 10^{-3}$

42977.text: As shown in the figure, a combination of a thin plano-concave lens and a thin plano-convex lens is used to image an object placed at infinity. Image from first lens will be virtual and on the left of first lens at focal length $40cm$. So the object for second lens will be $80cm$ from second lens which is $2{f}_{2}$. Final image is formed at $80cm$ from second lens on the right.

43818.text: A thermodynamic system is taken through the cyclic process $A B C$ as shown in the figure. The total work done by the system during the cycle $A B C$ is $\_\_\_\_$ J.

43818.sol:

Process B→C is isobaric: $W_{BC} = 300(5-5) = 0$ J

Total work done by system: $W = 600 + 0 - 300 = 300$ J

44634.subject: Physics
44634.text:
Two inclined planes are placed as shown in figure.
A block is projected from the Point $A$ of inclined plane $AB$ along its surface with a velocity just sufficient to carry it to the top Point $B$ at a height $10m$. After reaching the Point $B$ the block slides down on inclined plane $BC$. Time it takes to reach to the point $C$ from point $A$ is $t\left(\sqrt{2} + 1\right)s$. The value of t is _____ (use $g = 10m{s}^{- 2}$)
44634.sol:
From energy conservation at point $A$ and $B$,

$\dfrac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} = mgh$

$⇒ {v}_{0} = \sqrt{gh} = \sqrt{10 \times 10}$

$⇒ {v}_{0} = 10\sqrt{2}m{s}^{- 1}$

For $A \to B$

At $B, v = 0$

Acceleration of a particle moving on a smooth incline is $gsin\theta$. Therefore, along $AB$, $a = - gsin45 ° = \dfrac{- 10}{\sqrt{2}}m{s}^{- 2}$.

Using equation of motion,

$v = u + a{t}_{1}$

$0 = 10\sqrt{2} - \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{2}}{t}_{1} ⇒ {t}_{1} = 2s$

For $B \to C$

Using second equation of motion,

$s = u{t}_{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}a{t}_{2}^{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{10}{sin30 °} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(10sin30 °\right){t}_{2}^{2}$

${t}_{2} = 2\sqrt{2}s$

So total time $T = {t}_{1} + {t}_{2}$ $= 2\sqrt{2} + 2$

$= 2\left(\sqrt{2} + 1\right)s$

46331.subject: Physics
46331.text: In a mass spectrometer used for measuring the masses of ions, the ions are initially accelerated by an electric potential $V$ and then made to describe semicircular paths of radius $R$ using a magnetic field $B$. If $V and B$ are kept constant, the ratio $\left(\frac{\text{ charge on$ the $ion }}{\text{ mass of the ion }}\right)$ will be proportional to
46331.sol:
The radius of the orbit in which ions moving is determined by the relation as given below
$\frac{m v^2}{R}=q v B$
where $m$ is the mass, $v$ is velocity, $q$ is charge of ion and $B$ is the flux density of the magnetic field, so that $q v B$ is the magnetic force acting on the ion, and $\frac{m v^2}{R}$ is the centripetal force on the ion moving in a curved path of radius $R$.
The angular frequency of rotation of the ions about the vertical field $B$ is given by
$\omega=\frac{v}{R}=\frac{q B}{m}=2 \pi v$
where $v$ is frequency.
Energy of ion is given by
or
$\begin{aligned}
E & =\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \\
& =\frac{1}{2} m(R \omega)^2 \\
& =\frac{1}{2} m R^2 B^2 \frac{q^2}{m^2} \\
E & =\frac{1}{2} \frac{R^2 B^2 q^2}{m} \ldots(i)
\end{aligned}$
If ions are accelerated by electric potential $V$, then energy attained by ions
$E=q V\ldots(ii)$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$\begin{aligned}
q V & =\frac{1}{2} \frac{R^2 B^2 q^2}{m} \\
or\frac{q}{m} & =\frac{2 V}{R^2 B^2}
\end{aligned}$
If $V and B$ are kept constant, then
$\frac{q}{m} \propto \frac{1}{R^2}$

49766.subject: Physics
49766.text: An electron transition takes place from excited state to ground state in hydrogen atom, then
options: Its kinetic energy increases but potential energy and total energy decrease
Its kinetic energy, potential energy and total energy decrease
Kinetic energy decreases, potential energy increases but total energy remains same
Kinetic energy and total energy decrease but potential energy increases
49766.sol:
The total energy of an electron in the $n$-th orbit of a hydrogen atom is given by $E = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}$ eV.

The kinetic energy is $K = -E = \dfrac{13.6}{n^2}$ eV.

The potential energy is $U = 2E = -\dfrac{27.2}{n^2}$ eV.

When the electron transitions from an excited state to the ground state, the principal quantum number $n$ decreases.

As $n$ decreases, the value of $\dfrac{1}{n^2}$ increases. Therefore, the kinetic energy $K$ increases.

Since the total energy $E$ and potential energy $U$ are negative and their magnitudes increase, their actual values become more negative. Thus, both potential energy and total energy decrease.

Answer: Its kinetic energy increases but potential energy and total energy decrease

A polarized light of intensity \( I_{0} \) is passed through another polarizer whose pass axis makes an
angle of \( 60^{\circ} \) with the pass axis of the former. What is the intensity of emergent polarized light

According to Malus Law, we have
\[ I=I_{0} \cos ^{2} \theta \]
where, \( I \) is intensity of emergent polarised light; \( I_{0} \) is intensity of incident polarised light; \( \theta \) is angle between pass axis of
both polarisers
Here \( \theta=60^{\circ} \)
Therefore \( I=I_{0}(\cos 60)^{2}=I_{0}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{I_{0}}{4} \)
Thus, intensity of emergent polarised light from second polarizer \( =\frac{I_{0}}{4} \)

$\begin{array}{r}=\frac{1}{2}\left\{\left(1-\frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{7}\right)+\left(\frac{1}{7}-\frac{1}{13}\right)+\ldots+\right. \\ \left.\left(\frac{1}{n^2-n+1}-\frac{1}{n^2+n+1}\right)\right\}\end{array}$

given $\omega_0=0\begin{aligned} & \omega=50 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\ & \alpha=25 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}^2 \\ & t=\frac{\omega}{\alpha}=\frac{50}{25}=2 \mathrm{ s}\end{aligned}$

56004.text: The rate constant of a reaction is $k = 3.28 \times 10^{-4}$ s^{-1}$. Find the order of the reaction.$
56004.sol:
The unit of the rate constant $k$ for an $n$-th order reaction is given by (mol L^{-1}$)^{1-n}$ s^{-1}$.

Given that the unit of the rate constant is s^{-1}$, we can equate the powers of concentration:

$1 - n = 0$

$n = 1$

Therefore, the reaction is of the first order.

Answer: First order

59627.sol:
According to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle:

$\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$

$\Delta x \cdot m \Delta v = \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$

$\Delta v = \dfrac{h}{4\pi m \Delta x}$

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta v = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{4 \times 3.142 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 50 \times 10^{-12}}$

$\Delta v = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{5718.44 \times 10^{-43}}$

$\Delta v = 1.1594 \times 10^6 \text{ ms}^{-1} \approx 1.16 \times 10^6 \text{ ms}^{-1}$

Answer: $1.16 \times 10^6\ \text\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$

61272.subject: Mathematics
61272.text: The rate of disintegration of a radioactive element at any time is proportional to its mass at that time, where $k(k > 0)$ is the constant of proportionality. The time during which an original mass of 1.5 gm will disintegrate to a mass of 0.5 gm is $\ldots$
61272.sol:
Let $m$ be the mass of the radioactive element at time $t$.

The rate of disintegration is given by $\dfrac{dm}{dt} = -km$

$\dfrac{dm}{m} = -k dt$

Integrating both sides with appropriate limits:

$\int_{1.5}^{0.5} \dfrac{dm}{m} = -k \int_{0}^{t} dt$

$[\log m]_{1.5}^{0.5} = -kt$

$\log 0.5 - \log 1.5 = -kt$

$\log \left(\dfrac{0.5}{1.5}\right) = -kt$

$\log \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = -kt$

$-\log 3 = -kt$

$t = \dfrac{1}{k} \log 3$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{k}\log 3$

63158.subject: Mathematics
63158.text: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -13 \\ 5 & -10 \end{bmatrix}$ be two matrices. If the variables $x$ and $y$ satisfy the matrix equation $((A^{-1})^2 + B)\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$, then the ordered pair $(x, y) = $
63158.sol:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$

Determinant of $A$ is $|A| = (3)(-1) - (-4)(1) = 1$

The inverse of $A$ is $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$

Now, $(A^{-1})^2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 4 & -4 + 12 \\ 1 - 3 & -4 + 9 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 8 \\ -2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$

Adding matrix $B$:

64399.text: The co-ordinates of the foot of the perpendicular from the origin to the plane $2x - 3y - 6z = 49$ are...
64399.sol:
The equation of the plane is $2x - 3y - 6z = 49$.

The direction ratios of the normal to the plane are $(2, -3, -6)$.

The equation of the line passing through the origin and perpendicular to the plane is $\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{y}{-3} = \dfrac{z}{-6} = k$.

Any point on this line is of the form $(2k, -3k, -6k)$.

Since this point is the foot of the perpendicular, it must lie on the plane. Substituting these coordinates into the equation of the plane:

$2(2k) - 3(-3k) - 6(-6k) = 49$

$4k + 9k + 36k = 49$

$49k = 49 \Rightarrow k = 1$

Therefore, the coordinates of the foot of the perpendicular are $(2(1), -3(1), -6(1)) = (2, -3, -6)$.

Answer: $(2, -3, -6)$

Simplifying produces $x - 2y - 3 = 0$.

Substituting the previous result gives:

$20 + 6 \cdot 2 = 32$

65557.text: Series LCR circuit containing an a.c. source of 100V has a inductor and a capacitor of reactance $24\ \Omega$ and $16\ \Omega$ respectively. If a resistance of $6\ \Omega$ is connected in series, then the potential difference across the series combination of inductor and capacitor only is
65557.sol:
Given $V = 100\text{V}$, $X_L = 24\ \Omega$, $X_C = 16\ \Omega$, and $R = 6\ \Omega$.

The net reactance of the circuit is $X = X_L - X_C = 24 - 16 = 8\ \Omega$.

The impedance of the series LCR circuit is given by $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$.

Substituting the values, $Z = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10\ \Omega$.

The rms current in the circuit is $I = \dfrac{V}{Z} = \dfrac{100}{10} = 10\text{A}$.

The potential difference across the series combination of the inductor and capacitor is $V_{LC} = I \times |X_L - X_C|$.

$V_{LC} = 10 \times 8 = 80\text{V}$.

68968.text: Two thin lenses having $R_1, R_2$ as the radii of curved surfaces are kept coaxially together. Their power is proportional to
68968.sol:
Power of coaxial thin lenses

The power of a thin lens follows the lens maker's formula $P = (\mu - 1) \left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right), where $\mu$ is the refractive index and $R_1$, $R_2$ are the radii of curvature with proper sign convention.

For plano-convex lenses with curved surfaces of radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ respectively, the flat surfaces contribute 1/$\infty =$0$ to the curvature terms. The individual powers become $P_1 = \frac{\mu - 1}{R_1} and $ P_2 = $\frac{\mu - 1}{R_2}.

When placed coaxially in contact, the combined power sums to $ P_{$\text{total} } = P_1 + P_2 = (\mu - 1) \left(\frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$.

This simplifies to $P_{\text{total}} = (\mu - 1) \left(\frac{R_1 + R_2}{R_1 R_2}\right), showing $P_{$\text{total}$ } \propto $\frac{R_1 + R_2}{R_1 R_2}$,$$matching option D.

69150.subject: Physics
69150.text: A solid sphere rolls without slipping on an inclied plane at an angle $\theta$. The ratio of total kinetic energy to its rotational kinetic energy is
69150.sol:
For a solid sphere rolling without slipping, the velocity of the center of mass $v$ and angular velocity $\omega$ are related by $v = \omega R$.

The translational kinetic energy is $K_{trans} = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$.

The rotational kinetic energy is $K_{rot} = \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2$.

Substituting the moment of inertia of a solid sphere $I = \dfrac{2}{5} m R^2$ and $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$:

$K_{rot} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{2}{5} m R^2\right) \left(\dfrac{v}{R}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{5} m v^2$

The total kinetic energy is the sum of translational and rotational kinetic energies:

$K_{total} = K_{trans} + K_{rot} = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 + \dfrac{1}{5} m v^2 = \dfrac{7}{10} m v^2$

The ratio of total kinetic energy to rotational kinetic energy is:

$\dfrac{K_{total}}{K_{rot}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{7}{10} m v^2}{\dfrac{1}{5} m v^2} = \dfrac{7}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{7}{2}$

69750.sol:
The power radiated by a spherical black body follows the Stefan-Boltzmann law: $P = \sigma A T^4$, where $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $A$ is the surface area, and $T$ is the absolute temperature.

For a sphere, $A = 4\pi R^2$, so $P = 4\pi\sigma R^2 T^4$.

Given two spheres with different radii and temperatures radiating equal power, set the expressions equal:
$4\pi\sigma R_1^2 T_1^4 = 4\pi\sigma R_2^2 T_2^4$

Canceling the common factor $4\pi\sigma$ yields $R_1^2 T_1^4 = R_2^2 T_2^4$.

Solving for the ratio $R_1/R_2$:
$\left(\frac{R_1}{R_2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^4$
$\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^2$

The final answer is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

71506.sol:
During embryonal development in dicot angiosperms, the zygote divides to form a terminal cell and a basal cell. The terminal cell develops into an octant stage proembryo.

The upper tier of cells of the octant gives rise to the plumule and cotyledons.

The lower tier of cells of the octant forms the hypocotyl and a part of the radicle.

The basal cell forms the suspensor. The uppermost cell of the suspensor, which is situated just below the embryonal mass, is called the hypophysis.

The hypophysis undergoes divisions to form the remaining part of the radicle (root tip) and the root cap.

Answer: hypophysis

71651.subject: Chemistry
71651.text: Which one of the following compounds has the highest boiling point?
71651.sol:
Among isomeric amines, the boiling point decreases with an increase in the branching of the alkyl group.

Branching decreases the surface area of the molecule, which in turn decreases the magnitude of van der Waals forces of attraction.

n-Butylamine is a straight-chain primary amine and has the maximum surface area among the given isomers. Therefore, it has the strongest van der Waals forces and the highest boiling point.

Isobutylamine, sec-butylamine, and tert-butylamine have branched alkyl groups, leading to lower surface areas and consequently lower boiling points.

The order of boiling points is n-butylamine $>$ isobutylamine $>$ sec-butylamine $>$ tert-butylamine.

Answer: n-Butylamine

Water gas is a mixture of carbon monoxide $(\mathrm{CO})$ and hydrogen $\left(\mathrm{H}_2\right)$, typically produced through a process known as gasification. In this process, steam $\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right.$ ) is passed over red-hot coke (a form of carbon), which results in the following endothermic reaction:
$\mathrm{C}(\text{ coke })+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \text{ (steam) } \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}+\mathrm{H}_2 
This reaction occurs at high temperatures and requires continuous heating to maintain the reaction. The resulting water gas, composed of CO and  \mathrm{H}_2$, can be used as a fuel or as an intermediate in the production of other chemicals. It is an important industrial process for generating a synthesis gas that can be used in various applications, including the synthesis of methanol and hydrocarbons via the Fischer-Tropsch process.

76413.text: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the function $f(\mathrm{x})=\mathrm{x}(\mathrm{x}-1)(\mathrm{x}+1)$ ?
options: The local maximum value is larger than local minimum value
The local maximum value is smaller than local minimum value
The function has no local maximum
The function has no local minimum
76413.sol:
$f(x)=x(x-1)(x+1)=x\left(x^2-1\right)$
Differentiating, we get
$f^{\prime}(x)=x(2 x)+\left(x^2-1\right)=2 x^2+x^2-1=3 x^2-1$
Again differentiating
$f^{\prime \prime}(x)=6 x$
$\operatorname{At}^{\prime}(x)=0 \Rightarrow 3 x^2-1=0 \Rightarrow x^2=\frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow x= \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$
Maximum value of $f(x)=f\left(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}}\left(\left(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2-1\right)$
$=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}}\left(\frac{1}{3}-1\right)=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}}\left(\frac{-2}{3}\right)=\frac{2}{3 \sqrt{3}}$
Minimum value of $f(x)=f\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\left(\frac{1}{3}-1\right)=\frac{-2}{3 \sqrt{3}}$

Consider the function $f(x) = \begin{cases} 4(5^x), & x < 0 \\ 8k + x, & x \geq 0 \end{cases}$.

For $x < 0$, the function is given by $f(x) = 4(5^x)$.

To find $f'(-1)$, substitute $x = -1$ into the derivative:

$f'(-1) = 4(5^{-1} \ln 5)$

$f'(-1) = \dfrac{4}{5}\ln 5$

78176.subject: Mathematics
78176.text:
For the following two (02) items:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of the quadratic equation $x^2 + (\log_{0.5}(a^2))x + (\log_{0.5}(a^2))^4 = 0$, where $a^2 \neq 1$ and $\log_{0.5}(a^2) > 0$. Further, $\beta^2 = \alpha(\log_{a^2}(0.5))$.

What is $\beta$ equal to?
78176.sol:
Let $p = \log_{0.5}(a^2)$.

The given quadratic equation is $x^2 + px + p^4 = 0$.

The product of the roots is $\alpha \beta = p^4$.

We are given the condition $\beta^2 = \alpha (\log_{a^2}(0.5))$.

Using the properties of logarithms, $\log_{a^2}(0.5) = \dfrac{1}{\log_{0.5}(a^2)} = \dfrac{1}{p}$.

Substituting this into the given condition gives $\beta^2 = \dfrac{\alpha}{p}$, which implies $\alpha = p\beta^2$.

Substituting $\alpha = p\beta^2$ into the product of roots equation gives:

$(p\beta^2)\beta = p^4$

$p\beta^3 = p^4$

Since $p = \log_{0.5}(a^2) > 0$, we have $p \neq 0$. Dividing by $p$ yields:

$\beta^3 = p^3$

Considering real roots, we obtain $\beta = p$.

Substituting the value of $p$ back gives $\beta = \log_{0.5}(a^2)$.

78672.text:
Paragraph : The mean and standard deviation of 100 items are 50, 5 and that of 150 items are 40, 6 respectively.
Question : What is the combined standard deviation of all 250 items?
78672.sol:
Here,
$\begin{aligned}
& n_1=100, \quad \bar{x}_1=50, \quad \sigma_1=5 \\
& n_2=150, \quad \bar{x}_2=40, \quad \sigma_2=6
\end{aligned}$
Combined $\mathrm{SD}=\sigma_{12}=\sqrt{\frac{n_1\left(\sigma_1^2+\mathrm{D}_1^2\right)+n_2\left(\sigma_2^2+\mathrm{D}_2^2\right)}{n_1+n_2}}\begin{aligned}
\sigma_{12} & =\sqrt{\frac{100\left[5^2+(50-44)^2\right]+}{\frac{150\left[6^2+(40-44)^2\right]}{100+150}}} \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{100[25+36]+150(36+16)}{250}}
\end{aligned}\left[$\begin{array}{l}
$\mathrm{D}_1=\left(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_{12}\right) \\
\mathrm{D}_2=\left(\bar{x}_2-\bar{x}_{12}\right)$
\end{array}$\right]\begin{aligned}
& =\sqrt{\frac{100 \times 61+150 \times 52}{250}} \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{6100+7800}{250}}=\sqrt{\frac{13900}{250}} \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{1390}{25}}=\sqrt{55.6}=7.45 \cong 7.5
\end{aligned}$
Hence, combined standard deviation of 250 items $=7.5$.

85800.subject: Biology
85800.text:
In the axon of a giant squid neuron,
(i) The resting membrane potential is $-70$ mV.
(ii) At the equilibrium potential of $\text{Na}^+$ ($E_{\text{Na}^+} = +55$ mV) there is no net movement of $\text{Na}^+$ ions across the membrane.
In an experiment, when the axon is stimulated, the voltage-gated $\text{Na}^+$ channels open. The membrane potential peaks at $+30$ mV, where the resistance of the axonal membrane for $\text{Na}^+$ flow is $1 \times 10^6\Omega$.
The net $\text{Na}^+$ current ($I_{\text{Na}^+}$) across the membrane and the direction of ionic movement at the peak is:
options: $I_{\text{Na}^+} = 25$ nA; direction = out of the cell
$I_{\text{Na}^+} = 100$ nA; direction = out of the cell
85800.sol:
The net ionic current across the membrane is determined by the driving force and the resistance of the membrane to that ion. The driving force is the difference between the membrane potential ($V_m$) and the equilibrium potential of the ion ($E_{\text{Na}^+}$).

Given:
$V_m = +30$ mV
$E_{\text{Na}^+} = +55$ mV
$R_{\text{Na}^+} = 1 \times 10^6\Omega$

The magnitude of the driving force for $\text{Na}^+$ is:
$\Delta V = |V_m - E_{\text{Na}^+}| = |30 - 55| = 25$ mV

Using Ohm's law, the net $\text{Na}^+$ current ($I_{\text{Na}^+}$) is:
$I_{\text{Na}^+} = \dfrac{\Delta V}{R_{\text{Na}^+}} = \dfrac{25 \times 10^{-3} \text{ V}}{1 \times 10^6 \Omega} = 25 \times 10^{-9} \text{ A} = 25 \text{ nA}$

Since the membrane potential ($+30$ mV) is less positive than the equilibrium potential for $\text{Na}^+$ ($+55$ mV), the electrochemical gradient continues to drive $\text{Na}^+$ ions into the cell in an attempt to reach equilibrium. Thus, the direction of ionic movement is into the cell.

Answer: $I_{\text{Na}^+} = 25$ nA; direction = into the cell

85852.text: Mendel's law of independent assortment implies that

traits are encoded by independent genes.
alleles segregate independent of their location on the chromosome during gamete formation.
traits are always encoded by different chromosomes.
85852.sol:
Mendel's law of independent assortment states that when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, the segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair of characters.

This implies that the alleles of different genes segregate independently of one another during gamete formation. The allele a gamete receives for one gene does not influence the allele received for another gene.

Answer: alleles segregate independent of one another during gamete formation.

86065.subject: Chemistry
86065.text:
Consider the following complex ions:
$[\text{Ni(CN)}_4]^{2-}$, $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$, $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$, and $[\text{Co(CN)}_6]^{3-}$.
The complex ions that are expected to show diamagnetic behavior at room temperature are:
86065.sol:
For $[\text{Ni(CN)}_4]^{2-}$, the oxidation state of Ni is $+2$. The electronic configuration of Ni$^{2+}$ is $3d^8$. Since CN$^{-}$ is a strong field ligand, it causes pairing of electrons, resulting in $dsp^2$ hybridization. All electrons are paired, making it diamagnetic.

For $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$, the oxidation state of Fe is $+3$. The electronic configuration of Fe$^{3+}$ is $3d^5$. CN$^{-}$ is a strong field ligand, so the configuration is $t_{2g}^5 e_g^0$. It has one unpaired electron, making it paramagnetic.

For $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$, the oxidation state of Cu is $+2$. The electronic configuration of Cu$^{2+}$ is $3d^9$. It has one unpaired electron, making it paramagnetic.

For $[\text{Co(CN)}_6]^{3-}$, the oxidation state of Co is $+3$. The electronic configuration of Co$^{3+}$ is $3d^6$. CN$^{-}$ is a strong field ligand, so the configuration is $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$. All electrons are paired, making it diamagnetic.

Therefore, $[\text{Ni(CN)}_4]^{2-}$ and $[\text{Co(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ are diamagnetic.

Answer: $[\text{Ni(CN)}_4]^{2-}$ and $[\text{Co(CN)}_6]^{3-}$

91192.text: The value of $\lim_{n \to \infty}\dfrac{\left[x\right] + \left[{2}^{2}x\right] + \left[{3}^{2}x\right] +..... +   \left[n^{2}x\right]}{{1}^{2} + {2}^{2} + {3}^{2} +.... + n^{2}}$ is equal to (where $\left[x\right]$ represents the greatest integer part of $x$)
91192.sol:
Let $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{\left[x\right] + \left[{2}^{2}x\right] + \left[{3}^{2}x\right] +... + \left[n^{2}x\right]}{{1}^{2} + {2}^{2} + {3}^{2} +... + n^{2}}$

Now, we have,

$f\left(x\right) \le \dfrac{x + {2}^{2}x + {3}^{2}x +... + n^{2}x}{{1}^{2} + {2}^{2} + {3}^{2} +... + n^{2}} = x$

and, $f\left(x\right) > \dfrac{\left(x - 1\right) + \left({2}^{2}x - 1\right) + \left({3}^{2}x - 1\right) +... + \left(n^{2}x - 1\right)}{{1}^{2} + {2}^{2} + {3}^{2} +... + n^{2}}$

$= \dfrac{xΣn^{2} - n}{Σn^{2}} = x - \dfrac{6}{ \left(n + 1\right)\left(2n + 1\right)} \left(∵ x - 1 \le \left[x\right] < x, ∀ x \in R\right)$

Thus, we have,

$x - \dfrac{6}{\left(n + 1\right)\left(2n + 1\right)} < f\left(x\right) \le x$

Now, we have,

$\lim_{n \to \infty}x - \dfrac{6}{\left(n + 1\right)\left(2n + 1\right)} = x & \lim_{n \to \infty}x = x$

Hence, by Sandwich Theorem, we have

$\lim_{n \to \infty}f\left(x\right) = x$

102080.subject: Physics
102080.text: An ideal gas expands in such a way that its pressure is directly proportional to the cube of its density. During this expansion process, the temperature of the gas:
102080.sol:
Let the pressure of the gas be $P$, volume be $V$, and density be $\rho$.

Given that $P \propto \rho^3$.

Since the mass of the gas is constant, density is inversely proportional to volume ($\rho \propto \dfrac{1}{V}$).

Therefore, $P \propto \dfrac{1}{V^3}$, which can be written as $PV^3 = \text{constant}$.

From the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT$, we can substitute $P = \dfrac{nRT}{V}$.

Substituting this into the process equation:
$\left(\dfrac{nRT}{V}\right) V^3 = \text{constant}$

$T V^2 = \text{constant}$

This implies that $T \propto \dfrac{1}{V^2}$.

As the gas expands, its volume $V$ increases. Since temperature is inversely proportional to the square of the volume, the temperature of the gas decreases.

Answer: decreases

The average time taken by a moving particle between successive collisions or impacts is referred to as the mean free time $\left(τ\right)$.

The average distance a moving particle travels between successive collisions or impacts is referred to as the mean free path $\left(\lambda\right)$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{kT}{\sqrt{2}\pi{d}^{2}P}$

and ${v}_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$

So, the mean free time $τ = \dfrac{\lambda}{{v}_{rms}}$

Therefore, $τ ∝ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{T}}$

102435.subject: Physics
102435.text:
Two identical horizontal spring-mass systems, P and Q, each with a block of mass $M$, are oscillating with an amplitude $A$ on a frictionless surface. In system P, a small mass $m$ is gently dropped onto the block when it is exactly at its mean position and sticks to it. In system Q, the identical small mass $m$ is gently dropped onto the block when it is exactly at its extreme position and sticks to it.

Consider the following two statements:
Statement I: For system P, the amplitude of oscillation decreases, while for system Q, the amplitude remains unchanged.
Statement II: The time period of oscillation for system P increases, but for system Q it remains unchanged.

Choose the correct option from the following:
options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
102435.sol:
For system P, the mass $m$ is added at the mean position where the velocity of block $M$ is maximum. This is an perfectly inelastic collision. By conservation of linear momentum, $Mv = (M+m)v'$, so the velocity decreases. Since potential energy is zero at the mean position, the new total mechanical energy is purely the new kinetic energy, which is less than the initial kinetic energy. Thus, the new amplitude $A'$ is less than $A$.

For system Q, the mass $m$ is added at the extreme position where the velocity is zero. No kinetic energy is lost because the velocity is already zero. The potential energy of the spring remains $\dfrac{1}{2}kA^2$. Therefore, the total mechanical energy is unchanged, and the amplitude remains $A$. Hence, Statement I is correct.

The time period of a spring-mass system is given by $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m_{\text{total}}}{k}}$. Since the total mass becomes $M+m$ for both systems P and Q, the time period increases for both. Hence, Statement II is incorrect.

Answer: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

102891.subject: Physics
102891.text: An electric dipole placed at an angle of $60^\circ$ to a uniform electric field experiences a torque of magnitude $\sqrt{3} \text{ N m}$. What will be the potential energy of the dipole when it is aligned parallel to the electric field?
102891.sol:
The magnitude of torque experienced by an electric dipole is given by:

$\tau = pE \sin \theta$

Given that $\tau = \sqrt{3} \text{ N m}$ at $\theta = 60^\circ$:

$\sqrt{3} = pE \sin 60^\circ$
$\sqrt{3} = pE \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$
$pE = 2 \text{ J}$

The potential energy $U$ of a dipole in a uniform electric field is given by:

$U = -pE \cos \theta$

When the dipole is aligned parallel to the electric field, $\theta = 0^\circ$.

$U = -pE \cos 0^\circ$
$U = -(2) \times 1 = -2 \text{ J}$

Answer: $-2 \text{ J}$

103277.subject: Physics
103277.text: The variation of terminal voltage $V$ with current $I$ drawn from a discharging cell is plotted as a straight line graph. The line intersects the $V$-axis at $1.5$ V and the $I$-axis at $3.0$ A. The emf and internal resistance of the cell are respectively :
103277.sol:
For a discharging cell, the terminal voltage is given by the equation:

$V = E - Ir$

When the current $I = 0$, the terminal voltage equals the emf ($E$) of the cell. The graph intersects the $V$-axis at $1.5$ V, which represents the open-circuit condition. Thus, $E = 1.5$ V.

When the terminal voltage $V = 0$, the current is the short-circuit current, $I_{max} = \dfrac{E}{r}$. The graph intersects the $I$-axis at $3.0$ A.

Therefore, the internal resistance $r$ is:

$r = \dfrac{E}{I_{max}} = \dfrac{1.5}{3.0} = 0.5\ \Omega$

Answer: $1.5$ V, $0.5\ \Omega$

103296.subject: Physics
103296.text: A circuit consists of a single loop containing two cells and an external resistor of $3\ \Omega$. The first cell has an EMF of $10\text{ V}$ and an internal resistance of $2\ \Omega$. The second cell has an EMF of $4\text{ V}$ and an internal resistance of $1\ \Omega$. If the cells are connected such that their polarities oppose each other, what is the terminal potential difference across the $4\text{ V}$ cell?
103296.sol:
The two cells are connected in series but oppose each other. The net EMF of the circuit is the difference between their EMFs:

$E_{\text{net}} = 10\text{ V} - 4\text{ V} = 6\text{ V}$

The total resistance of the circuit includes the external resistor and the internal resistances of both cells:

$R_{\text{total}} = 3\ \Omega + 2\ \Omega + 1\ \Omega = 6\ \Omega$

The current $I$ flowing through the circuit is:

$I = \dfrac{E_{\text{net}}}{R_{\text{total}}} = \dfrac{6}{6} = 1\text{ A}$

Since the $10\text{ V}$ cell is stronger, it dictates the direction of the current. The current enters the positive terminal of the $4\text{ V}$ cell, meaning this weaker cell is being charged.

For a cell being charged, the terminal potential difference $V$ is given by:

$V = E + Ir$

Substituting the values for the $4\text{ V}$ cell:

$V = 4 + (1)(1) = 5\text{ V}$

Answer: $5\text{ V}$

103414.subject: Physics
103414.text: In the given circuit, if power rating of heater is 1000 Watt at 100 Volt, find the resistance R in figure so that heater produces power of 62.5 W.
103414.sol: Power rating of heater, $\mathrm{P}=1000 \mathrm{~W}$ Voltage rating of heater, $\mathrm{V}=100 \mathrm{~V}$ $\therefore$ Resistance of heater, $\mathrm{R}_1=\frac{\mathrm{V}^2}{\mathrm{P}}=\frac{(100)^2}{1000}=10 \Omega$ According to question, power dissipated in heater, $\mathrm{P}^{\prime}=62.5 \mathrm{~W}\therefore$ Voltage $\left(\mathrm{V}^{\prime}\right.$ ) across heater can be calculated as $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}^{\prime}=\frac{\left(\mathrm{V}^{\prime}\right)^2}{\mathrm{R}_1} \Rightarrow\left(\mathrm{V}^{\prime}\right)^2=\mathrm{P}^{\prime} \times \mathrm{R}_1=62.5 \times 10 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{V}^{\prime}=25 \mathrm{~V} \text{ (across heater) } \\ & \end{aligned} \therefore$ Voltage across $10 \Omega$ resistor, $\mathrm{V}^{\prime \prime}=100-25=75 \mathrm{~V}$ Current in $10 \Omega$ resistor $=\frac{\mathrm{V}^{\prime \prime}}{10}=\frac{75}{10}=7.5 \mathrm{~A}$ Current in heater resistor $=\frac{\mathrm{V}^{\prime}}{10}=\frac{25}{10}=2.5 \mathrm{~A}$ So, current in $\mathrm{R} \Omega=7.5-25=5 \mathrm{~A}$ Now, $\mathrm{V}=\mathrm{IR} \Rightarrow \mathrm{R}=\mathrm{V} / \mathrm{I}=\frac{25}{5}=5 \Omega$

104307.subject: Physics
104307.text: The electric field of a plane electromagnetic wave propagating in a non-magnetic dielectric medium with a refractive index of $3$ is given by $\vec{E} = 60\pi \sin(kx - \omega t) \hat{j}$ V/m. The average intensity of the electromagnetic wave is:
104307.sol:
The amplitude of the electric field is $E_0 = 60\pi$ V/m.

The average intensity of an electromagnetic wave in a medium is given by $I = \dfrac{1}{2} \epsilon v E_0^2$, where $\epsilon$ is the permittivity of the medium and $v$ is the speed of the wave.

For a non-magnetic medium, the refractive index is $n = \sqrt{\epsilon_r}$, so $\epsilon = n^2 \epsilon_0$. The speed of the wave is $v = \dfrac{c}{n}$.

Substituting these into the intensity formula gives:
$I = \dfrac{1}{2} (n^2 \epsilon_0) \left(\dfrac{c}{n}\right) E_0^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} n \epsilon_0 c E_0^2$

We know that $\epsilon_0 c = \dfrac{1}{\mu_0 c} = \dfrac{1}{120\pi} \Omega^{-1}$.

Substituting the values $n = 3$ and $E_0 = 60\pi$ V/m:
$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times \dfrac{1}{120\pi} \times (60\pi)^2$

$I = \dfrac{3}{240\pi} \times 3600\pi^2 = 45\pi$ W/m$^2$.

Answer: $45\pi$ W/m$^2$

105227.subject: Physics
105227.text: In a full-wave bridge rectifier circuit using four identical p-n junction diodes, an AC input is applied. During the positive half cycle of the input, two diodes are conducting while the other two are non-conducting. Let $W_{\text{cond}}$ be the depletion region width of the conducting diodes, $W_{\text{non}}$ be the depletion region width of the non-conducting diodes, and $W_0$ be the depletion region width of an identical isolated, unconnected diode. Which of the following relations is correct?
105227.sol:
In a full-wave bridge rectifier, the diodes that conduct during a half cycle are forward-biased. Forward biasing opposes the built-in potential, which decreases the width of the depletion region. Therefore, $W_{\text{cond}} < W_0$.

The diodes that do not conduct during that half cycle are reverse-biased. Reverse biasing adds to the built-in potential, which increases the width of the depletion region. Therefore, $W_{\text{non}} > W_0$.

Combining these inequalities, we get $W_{\text{non}} > W_0 > W_{\text{cond}}$.

Answer: $W_{\text{non}} > W_0 > W_{\text{cond}}$

111936.subject: Chemistry
111936.text:
Consider the following carbocations:
I. 2-Methylbutan-2-yl cation
II. 4-Chloro-2-methylbutan-2-yl cation
III. 2-Methylpropan-2-yl cation

The correct decreasing order of their stability is:
111936.sol:
The stability of alkyl carbocations is determined by the number of $\alpha$-hydrogens (hyperconjugation) and inductive effects.

III. 2-Methylpropan-2-yl cation (tert-butyl cation) has 3 methyl groups attached to the positively charged carbon, giving $3 + 3 + 3 = 9$ $\alpha$-hydrogens.

I. 2-Methylbutan-2-yl cation has two methyl groups and one ethyl group attached to the positively charged carbon, giving $3 + 3 + 2 = 8$ $\alpha$-hydrogens.

II. 4-Chloro-2-methylbutan-2-yl cation also has $3 + 3 + 2 = 8$ $\alpha$-hydrogens. However, the presence of the electronegative chlorine atom exerts a $-I$ (electron-withdrawing inductive) effect, which decreases the electron density on the positively charged carbon, making it less stable than I.

Therefore, the correct decreasing order of stability is III > I > II.

Answer: III > I > II

114928.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a reaction with rate constant $k = 2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$, the time required for the concentration of reactant to drop from $0.5 \text{ M}$ to $0.125 \text{ M}$ is exactly the same as the time required to drop from $0.1 \text{ M}$ to $0.025 \text{ M}$.

Reason (R): The unit of the rate constant indicates that the reaction is of first order, and for a first-order reaction, the time required for a definite fraction of reactant to react is independent of its initial concentration.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
114928.sol:
The unit of the rate constant ($k = 2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$) is $\text{s}^{-1}$, which confirms that it is a first-order reaction.

For a first-order reaction, the time taken for the concentration to reduce to a specific fraction is independent of the initial concentration.

In the first case, the concentration drops from $0.5 \text{ M}$ to $0.125 \text{ M}$, which is a reduction to $\dfrac{1}{4}$th of the initial value (i.e., exactly 2 half-lives).

In the second case, the concentration drops from $0.1 \text{ M}$ to $0.025 \text{ M}$, which is also a reduction to $\dfrac{1}{4}$th of the initial value (i.e., exactly 2 half-lives).

Since both cases require exactly 2 half-lives, the time taken is the same. Thus, both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

119274.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The reaction of propanone with dilute $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ at room temperature yields a ketol, whereas heating the reaction mixture yields an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketone.
Reason (R): $\beta$-hydroxy ketones readily undergo dehydration on heating because the resulting carbon-carbon double bond is isolated from the carbonyl group.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct.
119274.sol:
Assertion (A) is correct: Propanone reacts with dilute $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ at room temperature to form a $\beta$-hydroxy ketone (ketol), specifically 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one. Upon heating, this ketol readily undergoes dehydration to form an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketone (4-methylpent-3-en-2-one, also known as mesityl oxide).

Reason (R) is incorrect: The dehydration of $\beta$-hydroxy ketones is highly favorable upon heating because the resulting carbon-carbon double bond is conjugated with the carbonyl group, not isolated. This extended conjugation provides significant thermodynamic stability to the $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated product.

Therefore, Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.

Answer: Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.

125414.subject: Botany
125414.text: What is the first product formed when CO2 is fixed in the Calvin cycle?
125414.sol: CO2 is combined with H2O to produce (CH2O) n or sugars. It was of interest to scientists to find out how this reaction proceeded, or rather what was the first product formed when CO2 is taken into a reaction or fixed. Just after world war II, among the several efforts to put radioisotopes to beneficial use, the work of Melvin Calvin is exemplary. The use of radioactive 14C by him in algal photosynthesis studies led to the discovery that the first CO2 fixation product was a 3-carbon organic acid. He also contributed to working out the complete biosynthetic pathway; hence it was called Calvin cycle after him. The first product identified was 3-phosphoglyceric acid or in short PGA.

How many carbon atoms would a molecule have which after accepting (fixing) CO2 , would have 3 carbons (of PGA)?The studies very unexpectedly showed that the acceptor molecule was a 5-carbon ketose sugar – ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP). The scientists took a long time and conducted many experiments to reach this conclusion. They also believed that since the first product was a C3 acid, the primary acceptor would be a 2-carbon compound; they spent many years trying to identify a 2-carbon compound before they discovered the 5-carbon RuBP.

125656.subject: Botany
125656.text: If a plant is illuminated exclusively with monochromatic light of wavelength greater than 680 nm, which of the following physiological events will occur in its chloroplasts?
options: Both PS I and PS II will be functional, resulting in the synthesis of ATP and NADPH.
Only PS II will be functional, resulting in the synthesis of only ATP.
Only PS I will be functional, resulting in the synthesis of only ATP.
Only PS I will be functional, but neither ATP nor NADPH will be synthesised.
125656.sol:
The reaction centre of Photosystem II (PS II) has an absorption peak at 680 nm, while the reaction centre of Photosystem I (PS I) has an absorption peak at 700 nm.

When only light of wavelengths beyond 680 nm is available for excitation, PS II cannot be excited and becomes non-functional. Therefore, only PS I is functional.

Under these conditions, the electron circulation is restricted within PS I, forcing the system into cyclic photophosphorylation.

Cyclic photophosphorylation results in the synthesis of only ATP, without the production of NADPH + H+.

Answer: Only PS I will be functional, resulting in the synthesis of only ATP.

Recently, the concentration of green-house gases has started rising resulting in enhanced green-house effect that is resulting in increase the mean global temperature. It is called global warming. The various green house gases are $\mathrm{CO}_2$ (warming effect $60 \%), \mathrm{CH}_4(20 \%)$, CFCs (14\%) and nitrous oxide- $\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}(6 \%)$.

127232.subject: Botany
127232.text: What is the purpose of ex situ conservation?
options: To protect threatened animals and plants in special settings
To maintain animals that have become extinct in the wild
127232.sol: – In this approach, threatened animals and plants are taken out from their natural habitat and placed in special setting where they can be protected and given special care. Zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks serve this purpose. There are many animals that have become extinct in the wild but continue to be maintained in zoological parks. In recent years ex situ conservation has advanced beyond keeping threatened species in enclosures. Now gametes of threatened species can be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods using cryopreservation techniques, eggs can be fertilised in vitro, and plants can be propagated using tissue culture methods. Seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods in seed banks

129389.text: Assertion : Mylein sheath insulates the nerve fibre and prevents its depolarisation.Reason : Nerve impulses are conducted more rapidly in non - myelinated nerve fibres than in myelinated ones.
options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion
If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion
If assertion is true but reason is false
If both assertion and reason are false
129389.sol: In non-myelinated nerve fibres, the ionic changes are repeated over the membrane all along the length of the fibre. So, the action potential flows all along the membrane over the entire length of the fibre. But in myelinated fibres, the ionic changes and the consequent depolarisation can take place only at the nodes of Ranvier free from myelin sheath, because the myelin sheath between the nodes insulates the fibre and prevents its depolarisation. So, the action potential in effect jumps from one node to the next.This is called saltatory conduction of nerve impulses. Because of this, nerve impulses do not have to run all along the myelinated nerve fibre. This is why nerve impulses are conducted far more rapidly in myelinated fibres than in the non - myelinated ones.

129783.subject: Zoology
129783.text: Do mechanisms of breathing vary among different groups of animals?
options: No, they are the same for all animals
Yes, they vary depending on habitats and levels of organization
129783.sol: Mechanisms of breathing vary among different groups of animals depending mainly on their habitats and levels of organisation. Lower invertebrates like sponges, coelenterates, flatworms, etc., exchange O2 with CO2 by simple diffusion over their entire body surface. Earthworms use their moist cuticle and insects have a network of tubes (tracheal tubes) to transport atmospheric air within the body. Special vascularized structures called gills (branchial respiration) are used by most of the aquatic arthropods and molluscs whereas vascularised bags called lungs (pulmonary respiration) are used by the terrestrial forms for the exchange of gases.

130243.text: What are the three tiny bones present in each middle ear collectively called?
130243.sol: The Skeletal system is grouped into two main divisions - the axial skeleton which includes the bones that make up the central axis of the body such as the skull, spinal column, rib cage and the appendicular skeleton which includes bones of the upper and lower limbs and the bones that attach the limbs to the axial skeleton. Bones play a crucial role in supporting and providing structure to the human body. They also protect delicate organs, store minerals, and produce blood cells.The human body consists of 206 bones in total. These bones are grouped into two main divisions - the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton. The skull is composed of two sets of bones, cranial and facial, that total to 22 bones. The three tiny bones present in each middle ear, Malleus, Incus and Stapes, are collectively called Ear Ossicles.

131460.subject: Zoology
131460.text: How did Hershey and Chase separate the virus particles from the bacteria in their experiments?
131460.sol: Similarly, viruses grown on radioactive sulfur contained radioactive protein but not radioactive DNA because DNA does not contain sulfur. Radioactive phages were allowed to attach to E. coli bacteria. Then, as the infection proceeded, the viral coats were removed from the bacteria by agitating them in a blender. The virus particles were separated from the bacteria by spinning them in a centrifuge. Bacteria which were infected with viruses that had radioactive DNA were radioactive, indicating that DNA was the material that passed from the virus to the bacteria. Bacteria that were infected with viruses that had radioactive proteins were not radioactive. This indicates that proteins did not enter the bacteria from the viruses. DNA is therefore the genetic material that is passed from virus to bacteria
